shell-history-suggestions.title: Shell history: semantic command suggestions
shell-history-suggestions.summary: Type part of a command or describe an intent to select a suggestion from past commands.
shell-history-suggestions.plain_explanation: Like a history menu that understands meaning: code lists previous commands and Jev picks the closest to your intent. Code controls candidates, matching and display; the user accepts a suggestion into the command line.
shell-history-suggestions.mechanism: The pinned README describes a zsh plugin using the latest 100 distinct history entries, narrowing to prefix matches when available. A single prefix candidate skips the model. Otherwise Choice selects a command ID and Noul judges whether any candidate fits; thresholds gate suggestions and stale responses are discarded after input changes.
shell-history-suggestions.advantage: Supports intent descriptions beyond literal prefixes while restricting outputs to historical candidates. Like the predictive launcher it selects candidates, but operates on commands rather than files.
shell-history-suggestions.limitation: History can be stale or sensitive and is sent to the service as candidate data. A suitable suggestion does not establish safe execution; user review remains necessary. The README reports roughly 0.7–0.9 seconds per request, not the millisecond claims from other demos. The author presents an experiment, not evidence of daily use.
shell-history-suggestions.reported_result: The author shares a roughly 22-second demo and repository, then states that Amp produced the demo. The repository README explicitly says it uses fabricated command history.
shell-history-suggestions.media_note: The main video and the author’s Amp production video are one project. A demonstration with fabricated history is not a real-user-log evaluation.
shell-history-suggestions.source_notes: **Documentation review:** Read the [README at 4b2b75d](https://github.com/mrnugget/jev-shell-history/blob/4b2b75d26c0ccf5726263904514a22a8e11659ea/README.md), distinguishing prefix filtering, Jev candidate judgments and zsh acceptance. The plugin was not installed and local shell history was not transmitted.
shell-history-suggestions.review_summary: Pinned docs specify history candidates, prefix filtering, Choice/Noul gates and stale-result rejection. The demo uses fabricated history and reports 0.7–0.9 s latency; everyday adoption and long-term acceptance are not established.

calorie-notebook.title: Calorie Notebook: text-based food logging

calorie-notebook.limitation: No database, recipe handling or error evaluation against actual labels is disclosed; an author reply also notes limitations of model calorie estimation. Fast responses do not establish accurate calories or a reliable nutrition-measurement tool.

json-render-ui.title: json-render: assemble interfaces from component choices
json-render-ui.summary: Turn interface requests into constrained component layouts, including additions, removals and moves.

seo-internal-links.title: SEO internal links: match existing text to relevant pages

tax-doc-classifier.title: Tax Doc Classifier: label tax PDF pages

game-level-generation.reported_result: The author records five requests at 319–375 ms Jev latency and an estimated $0.00057 each, not a measured sub-100 ms system.
game-level-generation.media_note: The main video, implementation article and author’s state clarification form one case.
game-level-generation.source_notes: **Author article:** The [implementation write-up](https://www.spritefusion.com/blog/generating-game-level-in-real-time-with-jev) documents allowed surface types, widths, gaps, heights and a recorded response. This is public-design analysis; the game was not run.
game-level-generation.review_summary: The implementation article specifies state, finite terrain choices and code placement, with five measured requests at 319–375ms. This supports bounded terrain assembly, not asset generation, unrestricted game creation or long-term playability.

maxfusion-ad-classifier.title: MaxFusion: classify advertising creatives
maxfusion-ad-classifier.summary: Label ads by style and customer-journey stage for account-level analysis.
maxfusion-ad-classifier.plain_explanation: Like arranging ads in a labeled cabinet: Jev judges dimensions and code aggregates results. Labels do not establish campaign effectiveness.
maxfusion-ad-classifier.mechanism: The author reports classifying 1,891 Resilia ads by journey stage, style and other dimensions. Text extraction, visual preprocessing and label definitions are not fully disclosed.
maxfusion-ad-classifier.advantage: Compare with StealAds for ad organization. This reports a larger batch, but different data, labels and preprocessing prevent direct timing comparisons.
maxfusion-ad-classifier.limitation: Human-label agreement, campaign impact and full collection costs are absent. Announced MCP support is not confirmed as released.
maxfusion-ad-classifier.reported_result: The author reports 1,891 ads in 19 seconds for $0.12; not independently reproduced.
maxfusion-ad-classifier.media_note: A distinct author, product and video differentiate it from StealAds despite their shared purpose.
maxfusion-ad-classifier.review_summary: A specific ad-classification demo, with no validated label accuracy or complete preprocessing costs; batch size does not prove superiority over another tool.

danish-stock-backtest.title: Danish equities: a full-year historical strategy experiment
danish-stock-backtest.summary: Experiment with trading decisions on 2025 market data using news and other signals.
danish-stock-backtest.plain_explanation: Like working through an old market diary one day at a time. A valid backtest must restrict inputs to information available at each historical moment.
danish-stock-backtest.mechanism: The author cites market data, news, Wikipedia and Google Trends sentiment. Published in 2026 about 2025, it is cataloged as historical experimentation; time cutoffs and execution details are unknown.
danish-stock-backtest.advantage: Identifies multiple input sources and a year-long span, complementing the configuration-focused backtest interface.
danish-stock-backtest.limitation: Look-ahead controls, fees, slippage and reliable return statistics are missing. Token charges are not full strategy costs.
danish-stock-backtest.reported_result: The author reports 239 trading days, 8.1 million tokens and $0.32; not independently reproduced.
danish-stock-backtest.media_note: The roughly 22-second video is not evidence of current live-account trading.
danish-stock-backtest.review_summary: The dated 2025 run is a historical experiment with self-reported token cost. Point-in-time inputs, leakage controls, trading costs and validated returns are unspecified; it is not evidence of profitable live trading.

flappy-bird.title: Flappy Bird: navigate obstacles
flappy-bird.summary: Use Jev in controlling a bird through obstacles.
flappy-bird.plain_explanation: Think of repeatedly asking whether to flap now. This is an explanatory analogy; how this demo supplies state and schedules decisions is undisclosed.
flappy-bird.mechanism: The author posts Jev playing Flappy Bird without specifying observations, action frequency or whether the environment pauses for inference.
flappy-bird.advantage: A simpler action space than many character games helps study timing, but does not itself establish reliability.
flappy-bird.limitation: No multi-run scores, failure clips, costs or reproducible source. A successful clip does not establish completion rate.
flappy-bird.reported_result: The author supplies roughly 49 seconds of gameplay without a verifiable quantitative success rate.
flappy-bird.media_note: Cataloged as a distinct game task alongside other game-decision experiments.
flappy-bird.review_summary: A plausible short game-control demo. The effortless framing is impressionistic; observation format, timing, failures and repeated scores are not available.

script-code-review.title: Script.it: flag issues before writing review comments
script-code-review.summary: Score a git diff first, then ask a language model for explanations only when issues are flagged.
script-code-review.plain_explanation: Like marking suspicious changes with a checklist before asking a reviewer to explain them. This can avoid lengthy exploration but may miss deeper issues.
script-code-review.mechanism: The author replaces a multi-turn GLM/Grok/Gemini ensemble with direct Jev scoring of raw diffs, invoking an LLM for explanations after a flag.
script-code-review.advantage: Explicitly separates detection from explanation compared with agent-led review, and discloses the recall tradeoff.
script-code-review.limitation: The private set’s size and labels are unavailable. Zero false positives refers to tested developer-disputed findings, not a guarantee of no production errors.
script-code-review.reported_result: The author reports roughly 50× speed, 100× cost improvement and 75% confirmed-bug recall; the previous ensemble detected more bugs.
script-code-review.media_note: The source includes an image and workflow description. Results remain an internal author evaluation, not independent certification.
script-code-review.review_summary: The author discloses the workflow change and 75% recall trade-off. Private-data zero false positives and speed/cost ratios remain unverified, but are not presented as an equal-recall universal guarantee.

nifty-trading.title: Nifty intraday trading: an account demo with a stop-loss report
nifty-trading.summary: Demonstrate Jev-connected Nifty trading and report a triggered stop loss.
nifty-trading.plain_explanation: Like connecting decisions to orders with a stopping rule. Model judgments, broker execution and risk controls have separate roles; a video does not prove profitability.
nifty-trading.mechanism: The author claims a real Kotak account with ₹100,000 and 5× leverage. Strategy inputs, Jev candidates and order code are undisclosed; live-account status was not independently verified.
nifty-trading.advantage: Unlike speed-only trading posts, this discloses a stopped-out day and an author-reported adverse outcome.
nifty-trading.limitation: Accounts, fills and net returns are unverified. Leverage magnifies losses; one stop-loss report does not establish durable risk control.
nifty-trading.reported_result: The author says an initially profitable morning ended at the ₹1,000 hard stop, not an overall profitable day.
nifty-trading.media_note: The roughly 38-second video has a different author, market and execution venue from the Monad/Kuru bot.
nifty-trading.review_summary: The source reports a stop-loss after an initially green morning, not a profitable day. Account authenticity, executions and long-term risk controls remain unverified; the disclosure is more balanced than profit marketing.

downloads-organizer.title: macOS Downloads: organize files by rules
downloads-organizer.summary: Watch Downloads and move matching files to destinations defined by custom rules.
downloads-organizer.plain_explanation: Like a clerk recognizing an invoice and filing it: Jev judges rules, while the application moves and names files.
downloads-organizer.mechanism: The author demonstrates macOS folder monitoring and customizable rules, including invoice recognition and filing. They report no other LLM calls; extraction and filename construction are undisclosed.
downloads-organizer.advantage: Fits an ongoing local-file workflow rather than only batch classification. Box triage instead handles business reports in cloud folders.
downloads-organizer.limitation: Wrong moves or names can impair retrieval. Undo, conflicts, permissions and classification accuracy are undocumented.
downloads-organizer.reported_result: The author supplies a roughly nine-second demo without long-term or quantitative classification results.
downloads-organizer.media_note: Distinct from the same author’s X filter because both task and video differ.
downloads-organizer.review_summary: A plausible file-rule automation; extraction and filename construction are undisclosed, and no-other-LLM does not imply free-form generation by Jev.

color-judgments.title: Words and colors: visualize 16-color judgments
color-judgments.summary: Enter words and visualize the model’s judgments about colors.
color-judgments.plain_explanation: Like putting “tomato” into a box of 16 crayons: Jev weights color candidates and code visualizes the weights. It is not recognizing colors from photographs.
color-judgments.mechanism: Author replies specify 16 predefined static colors and link the palette. The complete display mapping is undocumented; separate RGB-mixing trials belong to the same experiment.
color-judgments.advantage: A smaller candidate set than pixel drawing offers direct semantic feedback for exploring word-to-visual interaction.
color-judgments.limitation: Constrained by palette and prompts, subjective associations have no single correct answer. This is not an image-recognition or color-science evaluation.
color-judgments.reported_result: The author shares roughly 65 seconds of interaction and palette details, without quantitative evaluation.
color-judgments.media_note: The 16-color explanation and later mixing discussion are merged rather than counted as multiple apps.
color-judgments.review_summary: The author discloses a fixed 16-color palette and rendering weighted probabilities. This supports word-to-palette associations, not visual color recognition or color-science accuracy.

x-reply-cleanup.title: X reply cleanup: flag low-value comments
x-reply-cleanup.summary: Identify suspected low-value replies to help clean up a post’s discussion.
x-reply-cleanup.plain_explanation: Like marking likely spam while letting the user correct mistakes. The author says corrections inform later decisions; storage details are unknown.
x-reply-cleanup.mechanism: The video shows checked/flagged reply counts, and the author describes Jev-based cleanup with false-positive correction. Local hiding, account blocking or other action semantics were not established; deleting others’ comments is not claimed.
x-reply-cleanup.advantage: More focused on replies than general feed filtering, with a correction mechanism; distinct from this author’s historical-post analysis.
x-reply-cleanup.limitation: Low-value judgments are subjective and error rates are unavailable. Correction feedback does not establish model training or cross-user learning.
x-reply-cleanup.reported_result: The author supplies roughly 15 seconds of video and a quick-build claim, without formal filtering evaluation.
x-reply-cleanup.media_note: The main video and correction follow-up form one application.
x-reply-cleanup.review_summary: The demo supports reply flagging and correction, but the precise action is unclear; using feedback on a later call is not evidence of model training or measured accuracy.

browser.title: Browser and computer control
browser.comparison: For browser loops, compare Browser Use and Stagehand: the former describes a dynamic DOM action space with text-generation fallback; the latter separates accessibility-tree observation from execution. For native apps, see CoreML/OCR. Cua currently offers a constrained semantic-action preview. agent-desktop retains an LLM for longer context; voice control and QA address different interaction needs. Runlayer emphasizes parallel sessions but lacks coverage and defect-detection evidence; Sac’s Calendar comparison focuses on one desktop task with an undisclosed observation interface. Neither action video substitutes for acceptance assertions. Tester Army targets web/mobile testing but its open-source release is unverified; ego lite focuses on product filtering with a hybrid stack. Browser Use now includes a same-project WebMCP comparison: task coverage and per-attempt success are distinct.
browser.flow: Observe the page or desktop → construct executable candidates → Jev selects → execute → observe again.
browser.analysis: DOM, accessibility trees and OCR are different observation interfaces. Keeping pixels local does not mean all content stays local. Browser Use still delegates text generation to an LLM. These designs come from author descriptions; unspecified encoding details remain unknown.
browser.evaluation: Compare the same read-only tasks using completion rate, steps, full elapsed time, total cost and recovery. Include unlabeled buttons, dynamic pages, dialogs and window changes. Do not compare one model decision with an entire task.

routing.title: Model, skill and tool routing
routing.comparison: Eve and Ephraim demonstrate model selection; Firstmate and local delegation address agent orchestration. Skillbox searches a skill library, Coding Garden connects everyday tools, and the Eve tool agent substitutes one stage of an existing system. ai-cli is an integration interface. These approaches can be combined. Hono JevRouter selects HTTP handlers using descriptions and the first qualifying route in registration order. Unlike model or skill selection, a routing error changes the response directly; it must not replace authentication. Codex Model Router selects a model and reasoning configuration each turn with documented fallback, but a user observed over-routing on easy tasks. Compare final quality, cache behavior and total bills, not classification speed alone.
routing.flow: Task text and candidate capabilities → Jev choice or scores → application checks candidates and constraints → invoke the selected model, skill or tool.
routing.analysis: Routing reduces the overhead of choosing an executor; the executor still does the work. Firstmate reports a small 25-task agreement study. Skillbox lacks retrieval-recall data. Deterministic invocation does not guarantee correct choices.
routing.evaluation: Use identical requests and measure routing suitability, final task quality, fallbacks, quota handling and total cost. Include requests with no suitable candidate.

review.title: Code quality and safety checks
review.comparison: Compare the 14-check PR reviewer, jev-review and jev-rabbit for explicit risks and escalation, iterative scoring and natural-language team rules respectively. Codebase classification examines overall structure. Command safety, jailbreak screening and upload checks guard different actions and need separate false-negative evaluations. The ESLint experiment judges snippet compliance; OpenCode permissions decide whether a tool action is allowed, questioned or denied before execution. They check different things and are not substitutes. Comment scoring separates accuracy from usefulness for clearer interpretation than one overall score, but currently shows only two trivial examples. ESLint checks snippets against rules, while PR tools cover broader changes. Compare their task scope and evidence size separately. Script.it scores diffs before generating explanations, reducing workflow overhead but recalling only 75% of confirmed bugs in its author evaluation. Compare both reduced false positives and increased misses with exploratory review.
review.flow: Code or proposed action plus explicit rules → several narrow judgments → combine in code → notify, block or escalate.
review.analysis: The PR reviewer publishes an uncertainty-escalation rule, making it easier to inspect than an overall score. jev-review feedback can guide iterations, but a high score is not a passing test suite. Cheap screening does not remove the need to assess error costs.
review.evaluation: Measure false positives and negatives by risk type against independently labeled data. Test insufficient evidence, adversarial instructions, conflicting rules and uncertain results. Retain human review and static-tool baselines.

data.title: Data classification and organization
data.comparison: Email classification and DuckDB handle batches of text; the paper example includes generative preprocessing; Jev + Kimi shows uncertainty escalation. Payee cleanup is extraction/normalization and support intent is multi-question judgment. Their metrics are not interchangeable. Predictive spreadsheets put classification intent in column headings and emphasize live feedback. Compare interface response separately from full-table processing costs when considering DuckDB-style batching. The four-model email demo exposes differences in waiting time, while the 500-email case emphasizes batch scale and reported cost. The former lacks standardized accuracy and configuration evidence; the latter lacks a cross-model comparison. Times from separate demonstrations do not establish a ranking. The food notebook turns text into calorie and nutrient values. Like predictive spreadsheets it prioritizes immediate feedback, but numerical estimates also require trustworthy data and error evaluation; classification speed is not numerical accuracy. New cases cover tax-page identification, Box incident triage, Downloads filing, OCR-based image organization, Gmail intent search and snack scoring. Tax classification documents rejection gates and separate test sets; most others offer author timings. Accuracy cannot be ranked across unrelated datasets.
data.flow: Raw text or tables → needed cleanup/summaries → Jev judgments → fallback for uncertain items → write results to an index or table.
data.analysis: The paper example separates summary costs from classification. The fraud example escalates uncertain emails to a larger model. Preprocessing and fallback both count toward total system cost. Payee candidate generation is unknown; do not assume Jev freely generates merchant names.
data.evaluation: Fix labeled data and splits. Report per-class precision/recall, throughput, per-item latency, retries and total cost. Fraud evaluation also needs realistic prevalence and separate false-positive/negative analysis.

content.title: Content and advertising analysis
content.comparison: Live analyzers provide writing feedback; bookmark-percentile prediction defines a more specific target; historical-post analysis supports retrospective review; ad analysis organizes creative material. Viral classifiers and the X-algorithm simulator have limited generalization evidence. JevMeter applies rules to speech, not validated fact-checking. MaxFusion and StealAds label ads with different batches and dimensions; SEO linking instead selects related pages and existing anchors. Labels, link relevance and business impact require separate evaluation.
content.flow: Text plus analysis dimensions → parallel Jev labels/scores → explicit aggregation rules → editing feedback, statistics or an analysis interface.
content.analysis: A low score is not the same as a false claim, and past popularity does not establish future reach. Historical analysis supports correlation; retrospective labels can leak outcomes. Claimed use of real X weights does not establish recreation of the live recommendation system.
content.evaluation: Hold out time periods and accounts; prevent outcome leakage. Check scoring stability, calibration, preprocessing costs and a precise target definition. Fact-checking additionally requires evidence retrieval and source verification.

filter.title: Webpage and feed filtering
filter.comparison: The X filter targets posts in a feed; Unclutter targets ads, banners and upsells across webpages. One classifies content, the other page elements, so their rules cannot necessarily be reused directly. Sponsor Skip targets spoken sponsorship along a video timeline rather than webpage elements; caption availability, transcription and boundary errors are distinct comparison dimensions. X reply cleanup targets comments and adds author-described false-positive correction. Compared with feed filtering, action semantics and feedback storage need clarification; flagging does not establish deletion.
filter.flow: Extract posts/elements → apply user-written semantic rules through Jev → hide, collapse or remove.
filter.analysis: Filtering depends on extraction and rule scope. Fast inference does not guarantee no flicker, false removals or broken interactions; page structures can change.
filter.evaluation: Compare false removals, missed targets, initial display latency and per-page cost on a fixed page set. Check normal dialogs, login, infinite scroll and undo behavior.

memory.title: Context and memory filtering
memory.comparison: Tool-history compaction filters the current conversation; memory retrieval filtering selects from an external memory store. Both reduce input at different stages. Evaluate retained information and task quality before comparing token reductions. Compact Adviser decides when to compact; the existing compactor decides what to compact; memory filtering decides what to retrieve. They act at different stages and can be combined; downstream task quality matters.
memory.flow: History or memory candidates plus current task → Jev relevance scores → select records → construct downstream context.
memory.analysis: Selecting original text and generating a new summary have different failure modes: selection can omit information needed later, while rewriting can distort it. The reported 94% reduction is one quick test, not a default compression target. Updated compaction-plugin sources show budget-fitted conversation context with tool-output bodies omitted; its recording animation makes no API calls. Evaluate size reduction, downstream task quality, cache rebuilding and total cost separately. The case includes the new usage report and reviewer critique.
memory.evaluation: Test delayed information needs, error recovery, old-decision tracing and cross-turn references in long tasks. Track recall, completion quality, filtering overhead and total tokens while retaining recoverable originals.

games.title: Game decisions and solving
games.comparison: Compare three Mario implementations: basic integration, a controlled structured-state/five-action Jev–Qwen demo, and a PPO implementation-effort anecdote. Pac-Man separates planning and execution; Pokémon reports longer progress; chess separates speed from strength; cube-solving code supplies the method. Other demos explore action spaces rather than establish a general leaderboard. Minecraft also uses layers, with local movement/aiming policies. Its performance belongs to the combined system; use the author’s original-speed supplement when comparing responsiveness. Flappy Bird focuses on action timing with sparse implementation details. Sprite Fusion selects terrain rather than player actions and documents parameters and request timing; evaluate reachability and playability rather than player scores.
games.flow: Environment state → adapter and legal action candidates → Jev choice → rule/executor checks → advance the environment.
games.analysis: Games can expose grid state, memory variables or other structured interfaces. The Jev–Qwen Mario post explicitly describes structured conversion and five choices; undocumented details elsewhere remain unknown. Cube algorithms come from code, illustrating how overall capability depends on the whole system.
games.evaluation: Fix environment versions, speed, action granularity and random seeds. Run repeated games and report wins, scores, total cost and stalls. State whether simulation pauses during model waits; separate decision latency from real game progress.

simulation.title: NPCs, driving and population simulations
simulation.comparison: Needs-driven NPCs explore behavior; the 500-agent demo explores throughput. Unpaused driving exposes latency constraints. The drone project provides code. Towns and fictional personas are storytelling or ideation tools, not evidence of real-world behavior.
simulation.flow: Simulation state and character goals → Jev decisions → simulated actions → updated state; an LLM may supply narrative reaction candidates.
simulation.analysis: FSD is the driving demo author’s label, not a reproduction of Tesla’s product or real-road capability. Overall API throughput differs from per-character update frequency. Fictional adoption intent is not user research. The drone repository specifies MuJoCo and separates fast control from slower model decisions, while disclosing the limits of its single-run comparison.
simulation.evaluation: Document environments, update rates, pause policy, network jitter and failure criteria. Track collisions, task success and character consistency over time. Compare synthetic-user findings with real research.

interaction.title: Real-time interaction and composition experiments
interaction.comparison: TypeGPU combines local perception with remote semantic decisions. Ask Jev exposes simple judgments. Word/character chat demonstrates selection loops; pixel drawing and RISC-jeV combine small judgments into outputs. These are conceptual examples, not established replacements for specialized models or programs. Other entries cover file selection, emoji suggestions, live shopping and voice-and-pointing canvas control. Their distinct tasks warrant separate cases. Both the canvas and TypeGPU combine perception with decisions, but one manipulates objects while the other changes audiovisual effects. Probably organizes judgments, branches and text generation into a small language. Its hosted site uses recorded playback, which must be distinguished from live local model calls when discussing responsiveness. Shell-history suggestions and the launcher both select a next step from candidates. The former documents thresholds in a pinned version but uses fabricated demo history; the latter selects files. Compare hit rates, acceptance and execution risks separately. json-render assembles interactive component trees, the color experiment visualizes 16-color judgments, and CNVS gates whether to respond to speech. They require structural/semantic checks, subjective matching and false-activation tests respectively, not just latency comparisons.
interaction.flow: Prepare finite candidates or atomic questions → Jev judges → code composes results → update interaction state or output.
interaction.analysis: Code assembles word and character choices into text; the API still returns judgments. RISC-jeV stacks logic-gate decisions and instruction interpretation to illustrate composition, not efficiency.
interaction.evaluation: Record vocabulary size, resolution or character count, loop count and full cost. Compare quality with deterministic code or specialized generators. Measure local perception, remote decisions and rendering separately.

finance.title: Trading and historical backtests
finance.comparison: Monad/Kuru demonstrates on-chain execution; the Nifty author claims live-account use and reports a stop loss. AI Hedge Fund and the Danish-equities experiment concern historical backtests. Execution demos require order, fill and risk-control verification; backtests require time-valid data and look-ahead controls. Speed and token bills do not establish profitability.
finance.flow: Market or historical information → strategy inputs and Jev judgments → simulator or executor → outcomes and risk records.
finance.analysis: Historical backtests and live fills are different evidence. Data timestamps, asset selection, generative models, costs and stopping rules affect results. This catalog did not connect accounts, execute trades or validate returns.
finance.evaluation: For offline or simulated reproduction, record time splits, fees, slippage, failed fills, position limits and maximum drawdown. Decisions per second alone have no investment significance.
